questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x,y)=2xy+{e}^{3x-y}.$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,3)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?
questions.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇\,f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }j \\  & =-(2y+3{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }i-(2x-{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }j \\ -∇\,f(1,3) & =-(2\cdot 3+3\cdot {e}^{3\cdot 1-3})\text{ }i-(2\cdot 1-{e}^{3\cdot 1-3})\text{ }j \\  & =-9\text{ }i-\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,3)$ in the direction of $-∇f(1,3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇\,f(1,3)‖ & =‖-9\text{ }i-\text{ }j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-9)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{82}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: In what direction does the function $g(x,y,z)={y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)$ increase most rapidly at the point $(1,1,2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z))⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z),\,2y,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1,2) & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi \cdot 1+\pi \cdot 2),\,2\cdot 1,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi \cdot 1+\pi \cdot 2)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi ),\,2,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi ,\,2,\,\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2\pi ,\,2,\,\pi ⟩.$

questions.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+3xy+2{y}^{2}$ increase most rapidly at the point $(2,1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xy+2{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xy+2{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =(2x+3y)\,i+(3x+4y)\,j \\ ∇f(2,1) & =(2(2)+3(1))\,i+(3(2)+4(1))\,j \\  & =7\,i+10\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $7\,i+10\,j.$

questions.problem: In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})$ increase most rapidly at the point $(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,j \\  & =2x{e}^{2y}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,i+2{e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})\,j \\ ∇f(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0) & =2(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2}){e}^{0}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+2{e}^{0}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j.$

questions.problem: Consider the function $g(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(-1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(-1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{3} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{x}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{(-1)^{2}},\frac{1}{(-1)}-\frac{(-1)}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{0(1)+0(-\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
